persons.note: HIS UNFINISHED LOFT IS THE PARCEL'S BEST DOCUMENTED LODGING. Andreas: 'Among these was P. F. W. Peck, who invited Mr. Porter to make his temporary lodging place and study in the unfinished loft of his two-story store'; and 'The first building in the rear of this store was the log house of Rufus Brown, where Mr. Porter found table board.' Three households and two buildings meet in those two sentences. He arrived in July 1831 with a stock of goods carried by schooner, per this project's building record. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Peck, P. F. W.” (tax_1833_083, line 135); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Peck, P. F. W.” (poll_1834_088, line 257). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 17 times, as “PECK P F W”, 1833-10-23 to 1836-09-05: 15 lots in the platted town — lot 1 of block 13 in the town the register codes CHIV (L1BL13CHIV, as printed); lot 1 of block 33 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL33CHIOT, as printed); lot 1 of block 55 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L1BL55CHIOT, as printed); lot 1 of block 6 in the town the register codes CHIOTVO (L1BL6CHIOTVO, as printed); lot 10 of block 9 in the town the register codes CHIV (L10BL9CHIV, as printed); lot 2 of block 10 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL10CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 28 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL28CHIOT, as printed); lot 2 of block 50 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L2BL50CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 10 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L3BL10CHIOTV, as printed); lot 3 of block 50 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL50CHIOT, as printed); lot 3 of block 55 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L3BL55CHIOT, as printed); lot 4 of block 41 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L4BL41CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 41 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL41CHIOT, as printed); lot 6 of block 44 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L6BL44CHIOT, as printed); lot 7 of block 26 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L7BL26CHIOTV, as printed) and 2 parcels of the school section — BL116 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read; BL6 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), as read, 0.00 acres stated in all, for $50426.00 (ls0319, ls0320, ls1412, ls1413, ls1414, ls1415, ls1416, ls1417, ls1418, ls1419, ls1420, ls1421, ls1422, ls1423, ls1424, ls1425, ls1426). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $49960.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. This person bid at the sale of the Fort Dearborn Addition, 10-24 June 1839, printed in Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 at pages 47-49. The bidder is printed as “P. F. W. Peck”. 1 lot row, $511 in all: block 8 lot 22 at $511 (f1839_lot0133, printed page 48). The sale table's own shorthand, recorded and not flattened: 1 carries the block number forward from the last row that printed one. What a match may carry, and it is short: that the man was in Chicago between the 10th and the 24th of June 1839 and bid at the Fort Dearborn Addition sale. It is written as 1839 evidence with describes_date 1839-06, never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on this alone. Under the ratified ladder a second contemporary source is what lifts projected_resident, and a land sale four years after the scene date is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not about July 1835. THE LOT IS NOT A LOCATION FOR 1835: the Fort Dearborn Addition is the Beaubien, or Reservation, lands, which in July 1835 were the garrison's ground and were not platted into lots at all. It places no house, no shop and no household in the town this project builds. No trade, no address in the town of 1835, no household and no house. The block and lot are the only location on the page, they are ground platted in 1839 out of the garrison's reservation, and they place nobody in the town of 1835. research_note: THE HOUSEHOLD AT THE CENTRE OF A THREE-WAY LINK. Peck's store lodged the Presbyterian minister in its loft and Rufus Brown's log boarding house stood directly behind it - so a single corner of South Water and LaSalle carries a merchant, a minister and a boarding-house keeper, all documented, all in this parcel. That is the density the inferred phase should expect to find everywhere and can only demonstrate here.

address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Peck, Philip F. W., real estate speculator, 242 Clark street'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. The street NUMBER printed against it is a number in the 1839 grid, a numbering this town's year does not have, so the street name crosses and the number does not. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.
